opening_message:
Ticket 1: Alexandra Johnson (employee ID E003) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E003.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Alexandra Johnson (E003) is a full-time Analyst. She requested admin access to Source Code. As a full-time employee, her maximum access is write, and admin is only allowed if her role owns the system (Source Code is owned by Engineer). Since she is an Analyst, admin is not permitted. Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E003 as a contractor with basic security training (note: this conflicts with HR's note of full-time). As a contractor, maximum access is read (write requires advanced training; admin never). She requested admin to Source Code, which exceeds the max, so recommend read.
reason: Alexandra Johnson (E003) requested admin to Source Code. HR's database, the authoritative source for employment type, shows she is a full-time Analyst. Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, so admin is not permitted for an Analyst. As a full-time employee without role ownership, her maximum access is write. Requested admin exceeds the maximum, so grant write. (Security's note conflicts on employment type, but HR is the authoritative source for employment status; either way, admin is not permitted.)

Ticket 1: Alexandra Johnson (E003) requests admin access to Source Code.

There are two notes with conflicting information:

Note 1 (HR agent):
- role: Analyst
- employment type: full_time
- recommendation: write
- Comment: full-time employee, max access is write, admin only if role owns system. Source Code owned by Engineer. Analyst doesn't own it, so admin not permitted. Recommend write.

Note 2 (Security agent):
- role: Analyst (not looked up, same as HR)
- employment type: contractor (looked up in own database)
- security training: basic
- recommendation: read
- Comment: Security DB shows contractor with basic training. Contractor max is read (write requires advanced training; admin never). Requested admin exceeds max, so recommend read.

So there is a conflict: HR says full-time, Security says contractor.

How should I resolve this? Let me think about the policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if they have advanced security training. Never admin.

The requested level is admin. Under either interpretation, admin is not allowed:
- If full-time Analyst: max is write (since Analyst doesn't own Source Code). Grant write.
- If contractor with basic training: max is read. Grant read.

I think the most defensible decision: HR's database is the source of truth for employment type (HR manages employment records). So she's full-time Analyst. Admin not allowed (role doesn't own system). Max is write. Grant write.

Let me submit write with reasoning.

But the policy says "If the requested level is at or below the maximum, grant the requested level. If above, grant the maximum." The maximum depends on employment type. 

Given conflicting info, which employment type do we accept? I'd say HR is the authoritative source for employment type. HR looked it up in their database. So full-time. Grant write.
